Deadlock: two or more threads/processes each hold a resource and wait for one held by another → circular wait, nobody proceeds, forever. Classic case: T1 locks A then wants B; T2 locks B then wants A. Requires all four Coffman conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break any one → no deadlock.

Avoidance, most practical first:
- **Global lock ordering**: always acquire locks in the same order everywhere (e.g. by address/ID) → kills circular wait.
- **Fewer locks**: hold one at a time, keep critical sections short, never call unknown code (callbacks, I/O, RPC) while holding a lock.
- **Acquire all-or-nothing**: `std::scoped_lock(a, b)`, or `tryLock` with timeout → on failure release everything, back off with jitter, retry (no jitter → livelock).
- **Avoid shared locks entirely**: immutable data, message passing/channels, atomics, single-owner threads.
- **Detect and recover**: DBs build a wait-for graph, abort a victim transaction → app must retry on deadlock errors. In SQL, touch rows/tables in consistent order and keep transactions short.

Gotchas: non-reentrant lock re-acquired by the same thread self-deadlocks; `await`/blocking on a result while holding a lock or on a single-threaded executor deadlocks without any second lock; thread-pool starvation (tasks waiting on tasks queued to the same full pool) behaves identically.
